resume: Translate entire PDF books and documents on your own machine — no data ever sent to the cloud.
besoin: Read a document in your language without handing it to an online service. toledo splits the PDF into chapters, translates it with a local LLM (Ollama), and can also convert it to Markdown, generate per-chapter study sheets or read it aloud.

demarche.declencheur: As a teacher, I regularly translate my own documents. The usual online tools raised one simple, non-negotiable question: where does this information go once it is handed to an outside service?
demarche.question: Can a document be translated and summarized properly, at zero cost, without the content ever leaving the machine — and can the same logic serve something other than translation?
demarche.conception: toledo runs on Ollama for the prototype — a local LLM rather than a cloud API —, but the architecture is built so another model can be plugged in later: nothing goes outside. Once that base was in place, the same mechanics made it possible to add two teaching features to try with my students: a document summary and a quiz generator. Going local was not only about cost — the privacy constraint dictated the whole architecture. It is also why toledo remains an application you install on your own machine, with no online version to try.
demarche.revele: Privacy is paid for in speed and in quality: a local model translates more slowly and needs more passes than a cloud one, and the trade-off only pays off when the document really is sensitive. The other surprise came from reuse — translation, summary and quizzes all rest on the same chapter-splitting brick: most of the work was in the pipeline, not in the features themselves.

resume: Project your retirement from a few parameters, without an intimidating spreadsheet.
besoin: Answer the simple question “does this hold up?”: savings, returns, horizon, withdrawals — and see how each assumption changes the outcome.

demarche.declencheur: Several friends were each going through a major change of course — and all landed on the same question: “How much do I need in order to retire?” Not a financial planner's answer with twenty assumptions, just a number to start thinking with.
demarche.question: How do you give a reliable order of magnitude, in a few minutes, with no financial jargon — and without forcing someone to book a consultation before they even know whether the subject is worth digging into?
demarche.conception: marbella stays deliberately simple: six sliders — current assets, annual savings, return, inflation, horizon, target withdrawals —, a transparent calculation whose formulas can be read inside the tool, and one clear result. No dashboard, no fifteen-scenario simulation. The goal was never to replace an adviser, but to give an honest starting point to a conversation that often never happens for lack of a first number.
demarche.revele: A “good enough” calculation people actually open beats an exact one they never do. The real obstacle was not the model's precision but intimidation: the first version hid its formulas, and making them visible — together with help on the retirement horizon, the notion everyone was conflating — did more for trust than any refinement of the maths.

resume: A growing hub of interactive companions for physical board games — round guides, searchable rules references — starting with Nemesis: Lockdown.
besoin: A dense board game's rules are easy to forget between sessions — instead of pulling out the rulebook every round, essen offers one interactive companion per game: a step-by-step round guide, a searchable rules reference, working offline once loaded (PWA). First game covered: Nemesis: Lockdown (Awaken Realms), whose 7-step Event Phase and many edge cases make it a good first test of this format. More games are coming, each with its own rules structure.
